<description>
{
 "summary": "Expands compressed IPv6 addresses into full eight-group notation when sending destination hostnames in SOCKS5 CONNECT requests. This works around an upstream Tor issue where relay exit nodes mistakenly parse `<name>:<port>` as a single IPv6 address if `::` absorbs the port as an eighth group, dropping the connection.",
 "problem": "Outbound connections routed through Tor SOCKS5 proxies fail with \"general failure\" for IPv6 peers whose addresses contain an inner `::`. Tor exit relays attempt to parse `<name>:<port>` as an address, causing the compressed address to absorb the port number and fail port extraction, dropping roughly 20% of IPv6 peers in addrman and ~29% of DNS seed IPv6 answers.",
 "evidence": [
  "Author references upstream Tor issue https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/issues/32314: Tor exit's `tor_addr_port_split` parses `2001:db8::1:8333` as a valid IPv6 address without a port and terminates the stream.",
  "Author measurement: \"About 20% of the IPv6 addresses in a gossip-filled addrman, and 29% of current IPv6 DNS seed answers, have an inner `::`.\"",
  "Author test against Tor 0.4.9.13 on mainnet: master failed to connect to four seed-provided peers with inner-`::` addresses (30 \"general failure\" errors), whereas this change allowed all four to connect and complete the version handshake."
 ],

<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.
